newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian govt bruised but not broken by protests.
newsitem.headline: Russian govt bruised but not broken by protests.

text.p: Russia's government is promising to work more closely with trade unions and employers after emerging bruised but not broken from a day of protests from one side of the vast country to the other.

The trade unions which organised Thursday's protests and strikes over wage delays and government policy said four million people took part. The Interior Ministry put the figure at 1.8 million, a tenth of what the unions had hoped for.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, able to breathe a sigh of relief that the protests did not turn violent and the crowds melted away, pledged to keep in touch with the unions better from now on.
"The strikes themselves and such actions will not help us," Chernomyrdin told a government session in remarks broadcast on Russian Public Television.

"They have never solved the problem and never will...The government must find a common language with the trade unions and the employers and operate in a framework of permanent dialogue with them. Without this we will hardly achieve an improvement."

The protests were the first big test of the new government which President Boris Yeltsin has gradually unveiled with Chernomyrdin, bringing in reformers to inject new vigour into economic reforms which have largely stalled.

Yeltsin, 66, has distanced himself from the failures of the government such as the huge backlog in wages and pensions which has left some public sector workers unpaid for several months. He has shifted blame squarely onto the government.
Much of the responsibility for tackling the problems now lies with two young liberal reformers, first deputy prime ministers Boris Nemtsov and Anatoly Chubais.
Chubais, accused by his critics of selling off state assets too cheaply when overseeing privatisation in an earlier role, was criticised by crowds across the country on Thursday.
But any fears that the protests could cause clashes similar to those in Albania, where violence erupted over the collapse of fraudulent savings schemes, proved wrong.
Thousands of police were placed on alert but no major violence or clashes were reported.
The dominant mood from Vladivostok, 7,000 km (4,500 miles) east of Moscow, to Russian cities on the Baltic Sea, was one of resignation.
Chernomyrdin had already soothed some people by vowing on Wednesday that the state and private employers would pay 11.8 trillion roubles ($2 billion) in back wages and pensions this month.

The government reshuffle also attacked part of the problem, although opposition politicians describe the changes as window dressing and doubt the cabinet's ability to improve the situation for millions of ordinary people.

"Changes in the government have convinced no one. This march is going from (the Pacific city of) Vladivostok to Kaliningrad (on the Baltic) and no one can stop it," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told reporters.
